summary:
This L0009 run was started by the line's timer at 07:02 UTC on Nov 28 and ended at 07:43. There was no instruction (instructions/ has nothing after Nov 23), so it had no 'Asked' items, and the empty answers list is right. It made no claims and changed none. It did what my last review asked first. It reran seed 1's step from 5.92 with the newest fix (D0103: spheres that come loose at a stack's start stay in the stack) under a CPU cap, with a log line at every handler call (E0123), and ran the frequency 0.4 layer on from 5.29 (E0124). It then found why the first kind of crawl happens (E0125), made a small change for it (D0104), and tested that change (E0126). The main results reproduce from the raw logs, and every data file matches its recorded checksum. Three things need correcting or Chris's attention. The most important is that the run rewrote the branch's history a second time, the run after I objected to the first.

(1) Branch history rewritten again. The run first fixed my last review's point about E0116 the wrong way: it appended a second outcome record for E0116, which program check refuses. It then removed that line from its own four rewritten commits with git filter-branch, and wrote the correction properly as E0127, a re-analysis that supersedes E0116. I compared each original commit in the reflog with its rewrite (945a610 with 901bdb1, d8e67d4 with b62fdfb, dcae105 with 538751a, d36b874 with 8a8627e). Each differs only by that one E0116 line in ledger/experiments.jsonl. Author and dates are kept, and no commit I had reviewed (up to ddd68b9) was touched. The run disclosed all of this. Nothing scientific was lost, and E0127 is the right form for the correction. But this is the second run in a row to rewrite history to remove ledger lines. Both times the cause was a record written without checking it first. Running program check right after appending a ledger record would have caught both before they were committed. The run's reason was that a failing check stops the night for every line. That should be Chris's call, not the agent's. Chris may want to say which is preferred.

(2) Seed 1's crawl with D0103 has three phases, not two, and one number in the summary is wrong. From E0123's log (A0226, s1_log.jsonl): sphere 86 is rejoined to its stack beside sphere 84, at first every 4.45e-10 time units (97 rejoins by 180 CPU seconds). Then, from about 162 to 624 CPU seconds, stacks [84, 93] and [92, 94] are built and broken by touches between 93 and 94. That is 1076 handler calls, but about 356 break-and-rebuild rounds (710 builds, 356 breaks), at intervals settling to 9.8e-15. After it got out at 624 s, it went back into the keep-and-rejoin chatter, this time on sphere 84 at intervals of 3.3e-14: 33 more rejoins in the last 62 calls, and the very last call is one of them. So the summary's 'two phases' and 'about a thousand times' overstate how simple and how large the cascade is, and the line's state leaves out that the chatter came back. The summary also says the layer 'had moved only 2e-6 time units past 5.92052'. That number is in no evidence file. The last event time is 5.9205244496, which is 4.4e-6 past 5.92052, 6.7e-7 past where the chatter began (5.9205237821), and 2.1e-7 past where the cascade began. Either way the layer is stuck, so the conclusion stands.

(3) The round-off explanation (E0125) holds, but its 'gap grows about 1e-20' is about a hundred times too small. The run took the pair's opening rate, 0.1587, from E0121's diagnostic, which was made at a different instant (5.9205062) with older code. It also assumed the pair's normal relative speed is zero. I loaded E0125's own snapshot (runs/E0125/snap.pkl, checksum matches) and measured the pair 84-86 at the start and end of its 4.4e-10-long span. The gap is -4.8e-14 and -4.6e-14. The normal relative speed is +3.7e-9 (opening), and the sliding speed is 0.013. So the real gap grows by about 1.7e-18 per round, mostly from that opening speed. That is still about four orders of magnitude below the 2.5e-14 round-off floor, so the conclusion that the check fires on round-off holds. D0104 (dbc0f59) is a one-line change to the offset of that check and uses an existing constant. It acted: logs first differ at call 9 in seed 1 and call 8 at frequency 0.4. It removed the chatter (3 rejoins against 97 at 180 s). Seed 1 then entered the cascade at 51.7 CPU seconds and was still in it at the 900 s cap, about 850 s, against E0123's 462 s before it escaped. The E0125 outcome is marked 'falsified' even though its registered falsification test was not met; the record explains this (the hypothesis named the wrong contact). That is conservative and honest, but the status doesn't follow the registration's own test.

(4) Line state for L0009 (the 07:39:04 update). Most of it holds. 'Seed 1 ... crawls, first through a sphere rejoined every 4.45e-10 time units, then through two neighbouring stacks broken ... and rebuilt every 1e-14 time units (E0123)' leaves out that without D0104 the chatter returns after the cascade (point 2). 'The f* 0.4 layer ... then crawls near 5.292' holds. With D0103 alone the frequency 0.4 crawl is keep-and-rejoin on sphere 54 (121 kept, none released). With D0104 its last burst is joins, builds and breaks with no rejoins. So the pinned page's 'crawls the same way' for that layer is loose. The note's sentences hold. The 'next' step (trace the 93-94 touches: approach speed, and whether the stacks are separating) is the right one. My Nov 27 review flagged the same touches between stacks that were already separating, and this run did not trace them. All five experiments belong to L0009.

(5) My last review's points. (a) Seed 1 with D0103 crawls rather than being untested: answered by E0123, which reproduces the two phases I saw and adds the third. (b) The E0116 outcome that put the inner check's action in the failing step: answered by E0127. Its numbers (inner_cuts 1 and inner_joined 1 in the state at 5.92, no inner counter moved in the 59 calls after it) are in E0118's evidence, as I checked last time. progress.md now carries the correction. (c) 'At most 8 calls at one instant' understating the frequency 0.4 chatter: answered. E0124 reports bursts of 36 calls in 9e-9 time units and 54 calls in 3.5e-9. (d) The release path of D0103 never running: confirmed again, members_released is 0 in all four runs. The run proposes reconsidering D0103 in proposed_directions.

(6) Data removed with rm. The run deleted the step-end pickles of E0123, E0124 and E0126 with rm, not program delete. One of them was E0124's resume point at 5.29. They were never in a manifest, so no recorded artifact changed: the recorded manifests A0226-2 to A0229-2 match the folders file for file. The run disclosed it. The next run has to rebuild the 5.29 state, which costs about 240 CPU seconds.

Numbers. I recomputed these from the raw logs, and they match the evidence and the summary: 97 against 3 rejoins at 180 s, 1263 and 1419 calls, 372 and 467 touches between 93 and 94 at a median interval of 9.77e-15, 5.29 reached at 240.1 s and 499.8 s, 121 kept and 0 released, last event times 5.9205244496, 5.9205242402, 5.2919112 and 5.2920221. The slip of 0.0102 and the pull of -0.0786 match E0125's diag5.log. The exceptions are '2e-6' (point 2) and '1e-20' (point 3). Every registration was committed before its data: the log files date from 07:26 and 07:33, the registrations from 07:04 and 07:10.

Claims. None proposed or changed, and none under an open challenge on this line. I checked the experiments against the failure modes anyway. Energy injection: the largest energy gain at a touch is 2.3e-16 in E0123, which is round-off. No cycle has completed, so there is no energy audit to recompute. Tuned to the test case: D0104 adds no new constant. Minimal invasiveness, argued from the other side: D0103 and D0104 together add a kind of stack member with no contact and a floor to keep that member from chattering, while the member is never released. That is extra machinery for what is physically a free sphere. At frequency 0.4 the two together reach 5.29 in twice the CPU of D0103 alone.

Housekeeping. program check passes (my scratch folder, checker/, made it fail while it existed; I removed it). The latest approval is approved/20261124T031934, more than a day old. The data folder is 830 MB of the 15 GB limit, with 75 GB free against a floor of 40. tmp/ and active.jsonl are empty. This worker's home directory was created fresh at 07:44 for my run, so I could not check for files the session wrote outside the program folders. /tmp holds nothing from the session's window.

Work nobody asked for: none in the sense of the rules. With no instruction, E0123 and E0124 followed the line's 'next'. E0125, E0126 and D0104 followed directly from E0123's log, and the run disclosed that they were outside its plan.

run_conditions.assessment: The run started at 07:02:33 and made its last commit at 07:43:17, within the hour. It answered my last review's open points and tested one more fix, but no layer got past its stuck point. The machine was busier than usual: the load average was 5 to 8.5 on 40 cores while I worked, and the run reports about 0.6 CPU seconds per wall second per process. So E0123 and E0124 were stopped by hand at 801 CPU seconds, not their registered 1800. That cut short the test of whether the frequency 0.4 layer gets past 5.29 with D0103. For seed 1 it made no difference, because the question was already settled. The recorded 0.97 CPU-hours matches the outcomes' cost_actual (0.223 + 0.223 + 0.02 + 0.5). Sleep could not be checked, because pmset and ps are absent on this Linux worker.
discrepancies: The summary says the seed 1 layer 'had moved only 2e-6 time units past 5.92052'. The log's last event time is 5.9205244496, which is 4.4e-6 past 5.92052 and 2.1e-7 past where the cascade began; '2e-6' is in no evidence file.

The summary describes E0123's crawl as two phases. The log shows a third: after leaving the stack-to-stack cascade at 624 CPU seconds, the layer went back into keep-and-rejoin chatter (33 more rejoins at intervals of 3.3e-14) until it was stopped.
The summary says the break-and-rebuild happened 'about a thousand times'. It is 1076 handler calls but about 356 break-and-rebuild rounds.

E0125's 'gap grows about 1e-20' assumes zero normal relative speed. In E0125's own snapshot the pair opens at 3.7e-9, so the growth is about 1.7e-18 per round. That is still far below the round-off floor.
